questions.q: What is a perfect square? Write any two perfect squares that are greater than 50.
questions.a: A perfect square is the square of a natural number. Two examples are 64 (8 x 8) and 81 (9 x 9).
s: States that a perfect square is the square of a natural number

True or False: A square tile of side 1.5 m covers more floor than a rectangular mat measuring 2 m by 1 m. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The tile covers 1.5 x 1.5 = 2.25 sq m and the mat covers 2 x 1 = 2 sq m, and 2.25 is more than 2.
s: Reason: compares the areas 2.25 sq m and 2 sq m

questions.q:

Reason (R): When a number between 0 and 1 is squared, the result is smaller than the number.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Since 0.3 is between 0 and 1, squaring it gives a smaller number.

questions.q: A square of side 12 cm is enlarged so that its area becomes 25 sq cm more than before. What is the side of the new square?
questions.a: 13 cm

questions.q: Find the area of each square. (a) side 17 cm (b) side 0.8 m (c) side 3/8 m (d) side 2.5 m (e) Which of the four areas is the area of a square whose side is a natural number? Name the area.
questions.a: (a) 289 sq cm (b) 0.64 sq m (c) 9/64 sq m (d) 6.25 sq m (e) 289 sq cm, because its side 17 is a natural number; the other sides are a decimal or a fraction.
s: (e) Names 289 sq cm because 17 is a natural number

questions.q: The gardening club of a school in Nashik has Rs 500 to buy seeds, which cost Rs 12 for every square metre sown. The club has marked two square beds: bed P with a side of 6 m and bed Q with a side of 2.5 m. The club wants to sow both beds. (a) Find the area of each bed. (b) Find the cost of seeds for bed P. (c) Is Rs 500 enough for both beds? If not, by how much is it short? (d) The club keeps bed P as it is and makes bed Q a smaller square whose side is a multiple of 0.1 m. What is the largest side it can choose and still stay within Rs 500?
questions.a: (a) Bed P is 36 sq m and bed Q is 6.25 sq m. (b) 36 x 12 = Rs 432. (c) Bed Q needs 6.25 x 12 = Rs 75, so both cost Rs 507, which is Rs 7 more than Rs 500. (d) Only Rs 68 is left for Q, so its area can be at most 68/12, about 5.67 sq m. 2.3 squared = 5.29 fits, but 2.4 squared = 5.76 does not, so the largest side is 2.3 m.
s: (a) Areas 36 sq m and 6.25 sq m
(d) Rs 68 left, so the area is at most about 5.67 sq m; checks 2.3 squared = 5.29 and 2.4 squared = 5.76 and gives 2.3 m

questions.q: A school can buy only one floor mat. Mat X is a square of side 1.6 m priced at Rs 150 for every square metre. Mat Y is a rectangle of 2.4 m by 1.1 m priced at Rs 160 for every square metre. (a) Find the area of mat X. (b) Find the area of mat Y. (c) Find the price of each mat. (d) The school has Rs 400 only. Which mat can it buy, and by how much does the other mat go above Rs 400? (e) Mat Y covers more floor. Is it still the better buy for this school? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 1.6 x 1.6 = 2.56 sq m. (b) 2.4 x 1.1 = 2.64 sq m. (c) X costs 2.56 x 150 = Rs 384 and Y costs 2.64 x 160 = Rs 422.40. (d) Only mat X, since Rs 384 is within Rs 400; mat Y is Rs 22.40 above Rs 400. (e) No. Y covers only 0.08 sq m more but the school cannot pay for it, so X is the better buy.
s: (a) Area of X is 2.56 sq m
(b) Area of Y is 2.64 sq m
(d) Chooses X and finds Y is Rs 22.40 above Rs 400
(e) Concludes that X is the better buy, giving the budget reason

questions.a: 1-S, 2-P, 3-Q, 4-R: 23 squared ends in 9, 18 squared ends in 4, 45 squared ends in 5 and 26 squared ends in 6.

questions.q: Without squaring, can 1,452 be a perfect square? Give a reason.
questions.a: No. 1,452 ends in 2, and a perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8.
s: Says that 1,452 cannot be a perfect square
Reason: its units digit is 2, which no perfect square has

questions.q: True or False: A number that ends in exactly five zeros can be a perfect square. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. A perfect square always ends in an even number of zeros, and five is odd.
s: Reason: squares end in an even number of zeros, and five is odd

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A number that ends in 6 is always a perfect square.
Reason (R): 16 and 36 are perfect squares that end in 6.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. 16 and 36 are squares, but 26 also ends in 6 and is not a square, so A is false.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: Four numbers are written on a board: 7,238; 3,00,000; 4,761 and 62,500. (a) Which of them cannot be perfect squares? Give the rule used for each. (b) For 4,761, use its units digit and the squares of 60 and 70 to find out whether it is a perfect square.
questions.a: (a) 7,238 cannot be (units digit 8) and 3,00,000 cannot be (five zeros, an odd number of zeros). (b) 60 squared = 3,600 and 70 squared = 4,900, so the root lies between 60 and 70; the units digit 1 means the root ends in 1 or 9. 61 squared = 3,721, but 69 squared = 4,761, so 4,761 is a perfect square.
s: (a) 7,238 (units digit 8) and 3,00,000 (odd number of zeros), each with its rule
(b) Root lies between 60 and 70 and ends in 1 or 9
(b) 69 squared = 4,761, so it is a perfect square

questions.q: Write the units digit of the square of each number, using only the units digit of the number. (a) 28 (b) 33 (c) 45 (d) 96
N is a two-digit number between 30 and 40, and the square of N ends in 9. Which list gives all the possible values of N?
questions.a: 33 and 37

questions.q: A 3-digit perfect square is the code of a school cupboard. Its units digit is 9, its digits add up to 16 and its hundreds digit is less than 3. Find the code. (a) Which units digits can the square root have? (b) Find the smallest and the largest 2-digit number whose square has exactly 3 digits. (c) List the numbers between these two that have a possible units digit, with their squares. (d) Use the digit sum to keep only some squares. (e) Use the hundreds digit to find the code and its root.
questions.a: (a) 3 or 7, since 3 x 3 = 9 and 7 x 7 = 49. (b) 10 squared = 100 and 31 squared = 961, while 32 squared = 1,024; so 10 and 31. (c) 13 squared = 169, 17 squared = 289, 23 squared = 529, 27 squared = 729. (d) The digit sums are 16, 19, 16 and 18, so 169 and 529 remain. (e) Only 169 has a hundreds digit below 3, so the code is 169 = 13 squared.
s: (a) Units digit of the root is 3 or 7
(d) Keeps 169 and 529 using the digit sum 16
(e) Chooses 169 (13 squared) using the hundreds digit

Consider the statements. Statement I: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36. Statement II: 41 is the 21st odd number. Statement III: Subtracting 1, 3, 5, 7, ... one after another from 50 reaches exactly 0. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. The sum of the first 6 odd numbers is 6 squared = 36, and the 21st odd number is 2 x 21 - 1 = 41. Statement III is wrong: 50 is not a perfect square, so the subtraction goes past 0 (after 15 the result is -14) without ever reaching 0.

questions.q: Without adding term by term, find 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 15.
questions.a: There are 8 odd numbers, so the sum is 8 squared = 64.

questions.q: True or False: Exactly 12 whole numbers lie strictly between 6 squared and 7 squared. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. 6 squared = 36 and 7 squared = 49, so the numbers 37 to 48 lie between them. That is 49 - 36 - 1 = 12, which is 2 x 6.

questions.q: Subtract the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, ... one after another from 16. (a) Show each step until you reach 0. (b) Hence say whether 16 is a perfect square and give its square root. (c) Does the same method show that 20 is a perfect square? Show the steps until the result goes below 0.
questions.a: (a) 16 - 1 = 15, 15 - 3 = 12, 12 - 5 = 7, 7 - 7 = 0. (b) It reaches 0 after 4 subtractions, so 16 is a perfect square and its root is 4. (c) 20 - 1 = 19, 19 - 3 = 16, 16 - 5 = 11, 11 - 7 = 4, 4 - 9 = -5. It goes below 0 without reaching 0, so 20 is not a perfect square.
s: (b) Perfect square with root 4, after 4 subtractions
(c) Shows that 20 passes below 0 without reaching 0, so it is not a perfect square

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The 25th odd number is 49.
Reason (R): The nth odd number is 2n + 1.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The nth odd number is 2n - 1, so the 25th is 2 x 25 - 1 = 49, which makes A true; R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: You are given 25 squared = 625. Using odd numbers, find the following without multiplying. (a) Which odd number is the 26th odd number? (b) 26 squared (c) Which odd number is the 25th odd number? (d) 24 squared
questions.a: (a) The 26th odd number is 2 x 26 - 1 = 51. (b) 26 squared = 625 + 51 = 676. (c) The 25th odd number is 49. (d) 24 squared = 625 - 49 = 576.

questions.q: A shopkeeper in Pune stacks tins in triangles. A stack with 1 row has 1 tin, with 2 rows has 3 tins, with 3 rows has 6 tins, with 4 rows has 10 tins, with 5 rows has 15 tins and so on. She notices that two stacks with consecutive numbers of rows hold a perfect square number of tins together. (a) How many tins are in a stack of 6 rows and in a stack of 7 rows? (b) Find the total of these two stacks and say which square it is. (c) A stack of 9 rows has 45 tins and a stack of 10 rows has 55 tins. Find their total. (d) A customer wants two stacks with consecutive numbers of rows that hold 169 tins together. Which stacks are these, and how many tins does each hold?
questions.a: (a) 21 tins and 28 tins. (b) 21 + 28 = 49 = 7 squared. (c) 45 + 55 = 100 = 10 squared. (d) 169 = 13 squared, so the stacks have 12 rows and 13 rows; they hold 78 tins and 91 tins, and 78 + 91 = 169.
s: (d) Stacks of 12 and 13 rows with 78 and 91 tins

questions.q: Find the sum 51 + 53 + 55 + ... + 99 without adding term by term. (a) Which odd number in the list 1, 3, 5, ... is 99? (b) Which odd number in the list is 49? (c) Find the sum of the odd numbers from 1 to 99 and from 1 to 49. (d) Use these to find the required sum. (e) Is this sum a perfect square? Use the squares of 43 and 44 to decide.
questions.a: (a) 99 is the 50th odd number, since 2 x 50 - 1 = 99. (b) 49 is the 25th odd number. (c) 1 + 3 + ... + 99 = 50 squared = 2,500 and 1 + 3 + ... + 49 = 25 squared = 625. (d) 51 + 53 + ... + 99 = 2,500 - 625 = 1,875. (e) 43 squared = 1,849 and 44 squared = 1,936, so 1,875 lies between two consecutive squares and is not a perfect square.
s: (e) Between 1,849 and 1,936, so not a perfect square

questions.q: True or False: A square mat has an area of 0.81 sq m, so its side is 0.09 m. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The side is 0.9 m, because 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81, while 0.09 x 0.09 = 0.0081.
s: Reason: 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81, so the side is 0.9 m

questions.q: A square sheet of tiles has an area of 70 sq cm. (a) Between which two consecutive whole numbers does its side lie? (b) Which whole number is the side closest to? (c) What is the side of the largest square tile of whole-number side that can be cut from the sheet?
questions.a: (a) 8 squared = 64 and 9 squared = 81, so the side lies between 8 and 9 cm. (b) 70 is closer to 64 than to 81, so the side is closest to 8 cm. (c) The largest tile has a side of 8 cm.
s: (b) Closest to 8, since 70 is nearer to 64

questions.q: Mohan says that the square root of (a + b) is always the square root of a plus the square root of b. Test his claim with a = 36 and b = 64, and then with a = 25 and b = 144. What do you conclude?
questions.a: For 36 and 64, the root of 100 is 10 but 6 + 8 = 14. For 25 and 144, the root of 169 is 13 but 5 + 12 = 17. In both cases the two sides differ, so the claim is false.
s: Concludes that the claim is false

questions.q: A square park has an area of 1,444 sq m. (a) Between which two multiples of 10 does its side lie? (b) Which units digits can the side have? (c) Find the side. (d) The park is fenced all round at Rs 15 for every metre. Find the cost of the fence.
questions.a: (a) 30 squared = 900 and 40 squared = 1,600, so the side is between 30 and 40 m. (b) The area ends in 4, so the side ends in 2 or 8. (c) 32 squared = 1,024 and 38 squared = 1,444, so the side is 38 m. (d) The perimeter is 4 x 38 = 152 m, so the fence costs 152 x 15 = Rs 2,280.

questions.q: The playground of a school in Madurai is a square of area 1,225 sq m. A runner practises by running round its edge. The school plans a second square ground whose side is twice the side of the first. (a) Find the side of the playground, using the squares of 30 and 40 and its units digit. (b) How far does the runner go in 3 rounds of the playground? (c) Find the side and the area of the second ground. (d) The sports teacher says the new ground has twice the area of the playground. Is she right? Give the number of times.
questions.a: (a) 30 squared = 900 and 40 squared = 1,600, and the area ends in 5, so the side is 35 m. (b) The perimeter is 4 x 35 = 140 m, so 3 rounds is 420 m. (c) The side is 70 m and the area is 70 x 70 = 4,900 sq m. (d) No. 4,900 / 1,225 = 4, so the area is 4 times as much, not 2 times.
s: (c) Side 70 m and area 4,900 sq m
(d) Not right; the area is 4 times as much

questions.q: A farmer will fence a square field of area 2,704 sq m. Shop A sells fencing only in rolls of 40 m at Rs 900 a roll, and the farmer must buy whole rolls. Shop B cuts fencing to any length at Rs 25 a metre. (a) Find the side of the field, using the squares of 50 and 55 and the units digit. (b) Find the length of fencing needed. (c) How many rolls must he buy from Shop A and what do they cost? (d) What does the fencing cost at Shop B? (e) Which shop is cheaper and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 50 squared = 2,500 and 55 squared = 3,025, and the area ends in 4, so the side is 52 m (52 x 52 = 2,704). (b) The perimeter is 4 x 52 = 208 m. (c) 208 / 40 is more than 5, so he needs 6 rolls, which cost 6 x 900 = Rs 5,400. (d) 208 x 25 = Rs 5,200. (e) Shop B is cheaper by Rs 200.
s: (e) Shop B is cheaper by Rs 200

questions.a: 3,844 = 2 x 2 x 31 x 31 = (2 x 31) x (2 x 31), so it is a perfect square and its square root is 62.
s: Pairs the factors, so it is a perfect square with root 62

questions.q: Find the square root of 4,900 using its prime factorisation. (a) Write the prime factorisation of 4,900. (b) Split it into two identical groups. (c) Write the square root.
questions.a: (a) 4,900 = 2 x 2 x 5 x 5 x 7 x 7. (b) 4,900 = (2 x 5 x 7) x (2 x 5 x 7). (c) The square root is 2 x 5 x 7 = 70.
s: (b) Two identical groups of 2 x 5 x 7

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 324 is a perfect square.
Reason (R): 324 ends with the digit 4, and 4 is a possible units digit of a perfect square.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. 324 = (2 x 3 x 3) x (2 x 3 x 3) = 18 squared, so A is true. R is also true, but a units digit of 4 only allows a square; it does not prove that 324 is one.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Find the smallest number by which 1,800 must be multiplied to make a perfect square, and the square root of the product. (a) Write the prime factorisation of 1,800. (b) Find the factor that has no partner. (c) Find the product and its square root.
questions.a: (a) 1,800 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 5. (b) One 2 has no partner, so 1,800 must be multiplied by 2. (c) The product is 3,600 = (2 x 2 x 3 x 5) x (2 x 2 x 3 x 5), so its square root is 60.
s: (a) 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 5
(b) The single 2 has no partner, so multiply by 2

questions.q: Find the smallest number by which 1,452 must be divided so that the quotient is a perfect square, and find the square root of the quotient. Use prime factorisation. (a) Write the prime factorisation. (b) Find the factor with no partner. (c) Find the quotient. (d) Find its square root.
questions.a: (a) 1,452 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 11 x 11. (b) The 3 has no partner. (c) 1,452 / 3 = 484 = 2 x 2 x 11 x 11. (d) The square root of 484 is 2 x 11 = 22.

questions.q: The stamp club of a school in Guwahati has two albums. Album A holds 6,084 stamps and Album B holds 2,646 stamps. The club wants to lay out all the stamps of an album in a square, with as many rows as there are stamps in each row. (a) Write the prime factorisation of 6,084. (b) Can Album A be laid out in a square? If so, how many stamps are in each row? (c) Write the prime factorisation of 2,646 and say whether Album B can be laid out in a square. (d) By what smallest number must the stamps of Album B be multiplied for a full square, and how many stamps are then in each row?
questions.a: (a) 6,084 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 13 x 13. (b) Yes. The factors pair up, so each row has 2 x 3 x 13 = 78 stamps. (c) 2,646 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 3 x 7 x 7. The 2 and one 3 have no partner, so it cannot be laid out in a square. (d) Multiplying by 2 x 3 = 6 gives 15,876 = 126 squared, so each row has 126 stamps.
s: (c) 2 x 3 x 3 x 3 x 7 x 7, and it is not a square because of the unpaired 2 and 3
(d) Multiplier 6, giving 126 stamps in a row

questions.q: A school wants to buy the smallest number of chairs that can be placed in a perfect square arrangement and can also be shared equally among 14, 15 or 21 classrooms. Use prime factorisation. (a) Find the smallest number divisible by 14, 15 and 21. (b) Write its prime factorisation. (c) Explain why this number must be multiplied by itself to make a perfect square, and find the number of chairs. (d) Check that this number of chairs can be shared among 14, 15 and 21 classrooms. (e) Write the number of chairs in each row of the square.
questions.a: (a) The smallest number divisible by 14, 15 and 21 is 210. (b) 210 = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7. (c) Each prime appears only once, so each needs a partner; the smallest number is 210 x 210 = 44,100 chairs. (d) 44,100 / 14 = 3,150, 44,100 / 15 = 2,940 and 44,100 / 21 = 2,100, all whole numbers. (e) There are 210 chairs in each row.
s: (c) Every prime needs a partner, so 44,100 chairs

questions.q: Which of these numbers is a perfect cube?
How many unit cubes make a solid cube of edge 6 units?

Consider the statements. Statement I: 500 is a perfect cube. Statement II: The cube root of 3,375 is 15. Statement III: A solid cube of edge 4 units is made of 64 unit cubes. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. 500 = 2 x 2 x 5 x 5 x 5 cannot be split into three identical groups, so Statement I is wrong. 3,375 = (3 x 5) x (3 x 5) x (3 x 5) = 15 cubed, and 4 x 4 x 4 = 64.

questions.q: Match each cube in Column I with its value in Column II. Column I: 1. 4 cubed   2. (-3) cubed   3. (2/3) cubed   4. (0.5) cubed. Column II: P. -27   Q. 64   R. 8/27   S. 0.125

s: Prime factorisation 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 x 7 x 7
Three identical groups of 2 x 7, so a perfect cube with root 14

questions.q: True or False: The cube of a negative number is positive. For example, (-6) cubed = 216. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. (-6) cubed = (-6) x (-6) x (-6) = 36 x (-6) = -216, so the cube of a negative number is negative.

questions.q: Find each cube. (a) 7 cubed (b) (-5) cubed (c) (2/5) cubed
Find the cube root of each number by splitting its prime factors into three identical groups. (a) 1,728 (b) 4,096 (c) 10,648 (d) 5,832 (e) 9,261
questions.a: (a) 1,728 = (2 x 2 x 3)^3, so the cube root is 12. (b) 4,096 = (2 x 2 x 2 x 2)^3, so the cube root is 16. (c) 10,648 = (2 x 11)^3, so the cube root is 22. (d) 5,832 = (2 x 3 x 3)^3, so the cube root is 18. (e) 9,261 = (3 x 7)^3, so the cube root is 21.

questions.q: In a craft class, Tara has 950 wooden unit cubes and wants to glue them into one solid cube. A solid cube of edge 9 units uses 729 unit cubes and a solid cube of edge 10 units uses 1,000 unit cubes. (a) How many unit cubes make a solid cube of edge 11 units? (b) Can she build a solid cube of edge 10 units with her 950 cubes? If not, how many more does she need? (c) What is the edge of the largest solid cube she can build, and how many cubes are left over? (d) After buying the missing cubes in part (b) and building the cube of edge 10, how many more cubes would she need to grow it to a cube of edge 11?
questions.a: (a) 11 x 11 x 11 = 1,331 unit cubes. (b) No. She needs 1,000 and has 950, so she needs 50 more. (c) The largest cube has an edge of 9 units, using 729 cubes, so 950 - 729 = 221 are left over. (d) 1,331 - 1,000 = 331 more cubes.
s: (c) Edge 9 units with 221 cubes left over

questions.q: A toy factory makes solid cubes from wooden blocks. (a) Write the prime factorisation of 1,372. (b) By what smallest number must 1,372 be divided to get a perfect cube? (c) Find the cube root of the quotient. (d) By what smallest number must 2,000 be multiplied to get a perfect cube? (e) Find the cube root of that product.
questions.a: (a) 1,372 = 2 x 2 x 7 x 7 x 7. (b) The 7s form a group of three, but the two 2s do not, so divide by 2 x 2 = 4. (c) 1,372 / 4 = 343 = 7 x 7 x 7, so the cube root is 7. (d) 2,000 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 5 x 5 x 5, and one 2 is left over, so it needs two more 2s: multiply by 4. (e) 2,000 x 4 = 8,000 = 20 cubed, so the cube root is 20.
